questions.question: An audit finds a password database where every stored hash string begins with the prefix '$2b$12$'. Which hashing algorithm produced these entries?
questions.explanation: The '$2b$' (or '$2a$'/'$2y$') prefix followed by a cost factor is bcrypt's modular crypt output format, so the format identifies the algorithm. bcrypt's tunable work factor keeps it slow against GPU brute-force attacks.

questions.question: A company rolls out logins where the user's device signs a per-site challenge with a private key that never leaves its secure hardware, so a look-alike phishing page harvests nothing reusable. Which standard enables this?
questions.explanation: FIDO2 (WebAuthn plus CTAP) registers a key pair per site and signs the server's challenge; there is no shared secret or password for a phishing page to steal or replay.

questions.question: On a PPP link, the authenticator periodically sends a random value and the peer replies with a hash of that value plus a shared secret — the secret itself never crosses the wire. Which protocol performs this exchange?
questions.explanation: A challenge-response hash where the password never traverses the link is CHAP's signature; PAP would transmit the password in cleartext, and the repeated re-challenges limit exposure to replay.

questions.question: Choosing a password hash for a new service, an engineer needs one that lets her raise the memory cost, iteration count, and parallelism independently to defeat GPU cracking rigs — the algorithm that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition. Which does she pick?
questions.explanation: Argon2's three independent knobs (memory, iterations, lanes) and its memory-hard design won the Password Hashing Competition; the Argon2id hybrid is the recommended variant for new applications.

questions.question: A banking app keeps verifying the signed-in user silently by measuring typing cadence, swipe pressure, and mouse movement instead of asking for credentials again. What class of authentication factor is this?
questions.explanation: Typing rhythm, mouse dynamics, and swipe patterns are behavioral traits measured continuously rather than one-time 'know/have/are' factors — this is behavioral biometrics.

questions.question: A web app issues session cookies that never expire. An attacker who sniffed one on public Wi-Fi a week ago still walks straight into the victim's account without a password. What attack did the missing expiration enable?
questions.explanation: Reusing a stolen, still-valid token to ride the victim's authenticated session is session hijacking; short token lifetimes and rotation after login would have closed the window.

questions.question: An enterprise 802.1X wireless deployment requires that BOTH the supplicant and the authentication server prove identity with certificates — no passwords may be used anywhere in the exchange. Which EAP method satisfies this?
alternatives: Extensible Authentication Protocol - Transport Layer Security
questions.explanation: Only EAP-TLS mandates a client-side certificate; PEAP and EAP-TTLS authenticate only the server with a certificate and run a password-based inner method inside the tunnel.

questions.question: A cloned magnetic-stripe card still works at a legacy terminal, but a copied chip card is useless because the chip generates a fresh cryptographic cryptogram for every transaction that the issuer verifies. Which payment standard is responsible?
questions.explanation: EMV chips produce a unique per-transaction cryptogram, so copying card data yields nothing replayable — unlike the static track data on a magnetic stripe that skimmers clone.

questions.question: After dumping NTLM hashes from one compromised Windows server, an attacker logs into neighboring machines by presenting a captured hash itself — never cracking a single password. What is this lateral-movement technique?
questions.explanation: In pass-the-hash the captured NT hash functions as the credential: NTLM authentication derives its response from the hash, so the attacker needs the hash, not the plaintext password.

questions.question: The same employee's login succeeds with just a password from her recognized office laptop, but demands an extra factor when attempted at 3 AM from a new country on an unknown device. What adaptive approach is the system using?
questions.explanation: Risk-based (adaptive) authentication scores context — device, location, time, and behavior — and steps up authentication requirements only when the risk score rises.

questions.question: A Kerberos user logs on once in the morning; all day the client obtains service tickets without re-entering a password by first presenting a credential the Authentication Service issued at login. What is that initial credential?
questions.explanation: The AS verifies the logon and returns a TGT encrypted under the TGS's key; the client presents the TGT to the Ticket-Granting Service for each service ticket, giving single sign-on.

questions.question: A biometric system is tested with 1,000 impostor attempts, of which 12 are wrongly accepted, and 1,000 genuine attempts, of which 30 are wrongly rejected. What are its FAR and FRR, respectively?
questions.explanation: FAR = false accepts / impostor attempts = 12/1,000 = 1.2%; FRR = false rejects / genuine attempts = 30/1,000 = 3%. The point where the two would be equal is the Equal Error Rate.

questions.question: An attacker steals a JWT and edits the payload's 'role' claim from 'user' to 'admin', but the API still rejects the forged request. Which of the token's three segments defeated the tampering?
questions.explanation: A JWT is header.payload.signature; the signature is computed over the encoded header and payload, so editing the payload without the signing key makes verification fail.

questions.question: After repeated push-bombing incidents, a CISO configures MFA so the login screen shows a two-digit number that the user must type into the authenticator app to approve. What is this anti-fatigue feature called?
questions.explanation: Number matching forces the user to transcribe a code shown only on the real login screen, so a victim cannot approve a push they did not initiate — defeating MFA fatigue/push bombing.

questions.question: An app must let users prove their password and derive a shared session key over an untrusted channel, while an eavesdropper who records the whole exchange gets nothing usable even for offline dictionary guessing. Which PAKE protocol does this?
questions.explanation: SRP performs a zero-knowledge proof of the password while establishing a session key; captured transcripts contain no verifier an attacker can grind against offline.

questions.question: A user receives dozens of unexpected MFA push notifications at midnight and finally taps 'Approve' just to make them stop. What attack has just succeeded?
questions.explanation: In an MFA fatigue (push bombing) attack, the adversary has the password and spams push approvals until the victim accepts one out of annoyance.

questions.question: A policy mandates passwords of exactly 12 characters drawn from a 64-symbol alphabet. If passwords are truly random, how many bits of entropy does each password provide?
questions.explanation: Each character contributes log2(64) = 6 bits of entropy, so 12 x 6 = 72 bits.

questions.question: To evade per-account lockouts, an attacker tries the single password 'Summer2025!' against 50,000 different usernames. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Password spraying tries one or a few common passwords across many accounts, the inverse of credential stuffing which replays leaked pairs.

questions.question: During Kerberos authentication, a client presents its ticket-granting ticket to request access to a file server. Which Kerberos component issues the resulting service ticket?
questions.explanation: The Authentication Server issues the TGT; the Ticket-Granting Server validates the TGT and issues service tickets for specific services.

questions.question: An administrator tunes a fingerprint scanner's threshold until its false acceptance rate equals its false rejection rate. What is the name of this operating point?
questions.explanation: The Equal Error Rate (or Crossover Error Rate) is where FAR = FRR; lower EER means a more accurate biometric system.
